Pull-away: on it, with it, pull away, shoot

In pull-away the muzzles first join the target, then pull ahead of it. It is widely taught in British coaching. Some sources call it the CPSA method (after the clay shooting association of England), while others use that name for swing-through, so ask your coach which is meant. Step by step, it looks like this:

  1. “On it”: the gun is mounted onto the target or its front edge; the muzzles touch it on its line.
  2. “With it”: the muzzles track the target for a moment at its speed, matching line and pace.
  3. “Pull away”: the gun accelerates smoothly ahead until the right lead picture appears.
  4. “Shoot”: the trigger is pulled while the gun is still accelerating or moving.
  5. Follow-through: the gun keeps going after the shot.

Strengths: you follow the target for a moment before pulling ahead. That gives you a feel for its speed, distance and path before you decide to fire, so the barrels stay well on its line. It suits long targets, quartering targets (flying at an angle away from or towards you) and rising targets. Because of the acceleration, the lead you see is smaller than with maintained lead.

Weaknesses: the amount of acceleration varies from target to target, so it takes practice to feel it. Tracking for too long becomes “riding the target”, and stopping the push gives a miss behind.

Coaches say “touch it and go”, “mount on it and push out”, or the four-beat “on it, with it, pull away, shoot”.

Key points

  • Muzzles start on the target (or its front edge).
  • Track at its speed, then accelerate ahead.
  • Trigger while the gun is still moving forward; then follow through.
  • Good line control; suits long, quartering and rising targets.
Stand Talk

  • Coach On it, with it, pull away, shoot.

    Meaning: Join the target, track it, accelerate ahead, fire.

  • Coach Touch it and go.

    Meaning: Meet the target with the muzzles and immediately start pulling ahead.

  • Coach You rode it too long.

    Meaning: The shooter tracked the target for too long before pulling away and lost the line or the moment.

  • Coach Mount on it and push out a bit more.

    Meaning: Mount onto the target, then pull a little further ahead before firing.

For the interpreter
  • Keep the four-beat rhythm when you translate: it matters more than the exact words.

Terms

  • Pull-away
  • Insertion point
  • Gun speed
  • Perceived lead
  • Quartering away
  • Riding the target
  • Follow-through
Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. In pull-away, what happens just before the trigger is pulled?

    1. The gun stops on the target
    2. The gun accelerates ahead of the target
    3. The gun drops below the target
    4. The gun waits at the break point
    Answer

    The gun accelerates ahead of the target

    The pull-away itself is the acceleration ahead; the shot is fired while the gun is still moving forward.

  2. The coach says “You rode it too long”. What went wrong?

    1. He stood too long on the stand before calling
    2. He mounted the gun far too early
    3. He tracked it too long before pulling away
    4. The trapper released the target late
    Answer

    He tracked it too long before pulling away

    “Riding the target” means following it too long, so it slows, drops or escapes and the line is lost.

  3. Compared with maintained lead, the perceived lead in pull-away is usually…

    1. smaller, because the acceleration adds lead
    2. larger, because the gun starts on the target
    3. about twice as large
    4. zero, with no gap at all
    Answer

    smaller, because the acceleration adds lead

    The brief acceleration carries the gun forward during the shot delay, so less gap needs to be seen.
